research_habits: **The proposed algorithm must be sufficiently innovative and original**, and the work of others must be properly cited.
Analyze why top models excel, maybe integrate their strengths to innovate, **copying is strictly prohibited.**

From Hypothesis to Experiment: Start with validated or pending hypotheses to design ingenious model structures and experimental strategies. Based on observed real-world results, confirm relevant hypotheses and discover interesting phenomena.
Match algorithms to physical reality: Consider the actual object behind the data. Models suited for crystals/alloys may not fit p-SMILES polymer datasets. Avoid blind cross-application

Negative results are valuable — attention and virtual node increasing overfitting is an important finding that prevents wasted effort on similar incremental approaches. Document and internalize negative results with the same rigor as positive ones.

Simple baselines can be surprisingly strong — GIN+Trimer outperformed all 6 more complex combinations. Always establish simple baselines before adding complexity, and evaluate whether complexity actually improves the overfitting gap (train-test RMSE difference), not just train RMSE.

Small-Graph Paradox lesson: On graphs where MPNN already reaches all nodes (avg shortest path < MPNN depth), Transformer attention is redundant overhead that increases overfitting without adding predictive value. Match architecture to graph scale — assess reachability before adding global attention. GPS-SPSE-Trimer=54.41 confirmed this on polymer trimers (30-60 nodes).

When multiple approaches fail on the same problem, pivot to fundamentally different strategies rather than continuing to tweak the same approach family. After 3 days of failed attempts (GPS, JEPA, PCR, PerioGT-Lite), the simple GIN + contrastive pre-training paradigm is exhausted. Pivot to PGFT or path encoding.
anti_self_deception: Zero Fabrication: Absolutely no hallucinations or fabrication of non-factual information. If an experiment fails or falls short of expectations, report it honestly; failure is also meaningful.

The overfitting gap diagnostic: never celebrate lower train RMSE if test RMSE increases. More expressive models that reduce train RMSE but increase test RMSE are memorizing, not learning. The overfitting gap (train RMSE - test RMSE) is the honest metric of generalization.

SSL Collapse Prevention lesson: JEPA-style EMA+MSE prediction converges to trivial constant-output solution without explicit variance/covariance regularization (VICReg). Contrastive learning (InfoNCE) naturally prevents collapse via negative pairs. For practical pre-training, prefer contrastive approaches over JEPA unless VICReg is carefully implemented. Day 2 JEPA collapse confirmed this.

Single-seed results are UNRELIABLE for contrastive pre-training: The PerioGT-Lite 50% corruption result (49.83) was a statistical fluctuation that disappeared under multi-seed verification (baseline 52.49±1.25 vs pre-trained 52.92±0.29). ALWAYS verify with ≥3 seeds before claiming any improvement. This is now a MANDATORY requirement.

Augmentation Difficulty Sweet Spot is Too Narrow: The cos_sim of positive pairs must be in a very narrow range (0.88-0.93) for contrastive pre-training to help on polymer graphs. Outside this range, it either provides no signal (too easy, cos_sim>0.95) or causes negative transfer (too hard, cos_sim<0.75). The relationship is also non-monotonic (40% corruption HURTS while 50% helps marginally), making hyperparameter optimization impractical.
learning_discipline: Paper Selection: Select 0-2 papers from the pool and 0-2 papers from arXiv. Do not select duplicate or overly similar papers.
Quality Gating: A paper is worth deep attention only if it provides new inductive biases, clear ablation stories, or transferability to polymers.

Periodicity Priors are Essential lesson: Generic SSL (random masking, random contrastive pairs) provides regularization but not domain-specific knowledge. The augmentation strategy must encode the domain's physical priors. For polymers, periodic augmentation (different fragments from the same chain) is essential. BUT: even PA augmentation doesn't consistently help on simple GIN (PerioGT-Lite FAILED). The issue may be that simple GIN can't effectively USE the learned priors, not that the priors aren't learned.

Implementation Consistency lesson: Pre-training and fine-tuning must use EXACTLY the same architecture (dropout rate, pooling method, normalization). Mismatches cause catastrophic degradation (~50 RMSE points observed). This is a non-negotiable engineering requirement.

Contrastive Pre-training on Simple GIN is Insufficient: PerioGT-Lite comprehensively tested 9 augmentation strategies with perfect implementation consistency. None consistently beat baseline. The simple GIN architecture ceiling (~51 RMSE) cannot be broken by any pre-training strategy. Pre-training provides variance reduction but not mean improvement. This suggests the architecture is too limited to benefit from richer representations.
content.High-ROI Experimentation: Prioritize performance given moderate hardware (11GB VRAM per GPU). Never under-train to save compute—it masks true algorithmic potential. Maximize Scientific Increment per Compute Unit. After 3 days of failed attempts on the same problem (closing the 50→30 gap with simple GIN + contrastive), pivot to fundamentally different approaches: (1) PGFT prompt-guided fine-tuning — use pre-trained representation as conditioning signal, not just initialization, (2) Path/distance encoding — add explicit structural information to node features, (3) Consider whether the simple GIN ceiling itself needs to be broken with a different architecture family that can actually USE pre-trained representations.

memory.abstract: The Contrastive Difficulty Trap: Both in-training (PCR-v2) and pre-training (PerioGT-Lite) contrastive approaches failed on polymer graphs, revealing a fundamental three-zone augmentation difficulty spectrum. Easy positives (cos_sim >0.93) are redundant — monomer-trimer pairs share substructure and are trivially aligned (0.94-0.97 at init). Hard positives (cos_sim <0.80) cause negative transfer — shifted-RU and monomer-dimer pairs destroy chemical semantics. The sweet spot (cos_sim 0.88-0.93) is too narrow and non-monotonic (40% corruption HURTS while 50% helps marginally). MoCL's bioisostere substitution lesson confirms: domain-aware augmentation must create HARD positives that are structurally different but semantically equivalent. Pre-training provides variance reduction (std 0.29 vs 1.25) but NOT mean improvement — the simple GIN architecture cannot USE periodicity priors regardless of how they're injected.
memory.keyword: contrastive difficulty trap, augmentation spectrum, easy positives, hard positives, sweet spot, variance reduction, MoCL, PCR-v2, PerioGT-Lite

consensus: PCR-v2 (mem_109) and PerioGT-Lite (mem_112) both failed comprehensively, confirming that contrastive learning — whether in-training on 7170 labeled samples or pre-training on 300K PI1M samples — cannot close the 50→30 gap with simple GIN backbone. The failures share a common root: the augmentation difficulty spectrum has a narrow, non-monotonic sweet spot that makes contrastive learning impractical for polymer graphs.

MoCL (mem_107) validates the principle that contrastive learning needs HARD positives — structurally different but semantically equivalent. Bioisostere substitution creates HARD positives by replacing substructures with chemically similar but structurally different fragments (cos_sim in useful range). Our monomer-trimer pairs are EASY positives (cos_sim 0.94-0.97) because they share the same molecular substructure, making InfoNCE trivially satisfied (mem_109). This is the same lesson from a different domain.

The augmentation difficulty spectrum mapped by PerioGT-Lite (mem_112) across 9 strategies reveals three zones: (1) Too Easy (cos_sim >0.93): monomer-trimer=0.98, hybrid corrupt=0.97 — contrastive objective trivially satisfied, no learning signal. (2) Too Hard (cos_sim <0.80): shifted-RU=0.70, monomer-dimer=0.68 — negative transfer, encoder learns to match unrelated structures. (3) Sweet Spot (cos_sim 0.88-0.93): edge+feat masking — marginal improvement but fragile. The sweet spot is extremely narrow (~0.05 cos_sim range) and non-monotonic (40% corruption at 0.893 HURTS while 50% at 0.880 helps marginally).

PerioGT-Lite's multi-seed verification (mem_112) confirmed that the best single-seed result (49.83 with 50% corruption) was a statistical fluctuation. Multi-seed: baseline 52.49±1.25 vs pre-trained 52.92±0.29 (p=0.53). Pre-training reduces variance (std 0.29 vs 1.25) but doesn't improve mean RMSE. This is a critical anti-self-deception finding (mem_114): single-seed results for contrastive pre-training are unreliable.
conflicts: The Day 2 Pre-training Paradox integration (mem_100) hypothesized that PerioGT-style PA-based contrastive pre-training on PI1M would close the gap because it provides (a) massive negative pair diversity, (b) pre-training on diverse polymer structures, (c) periodicity priors through different RU views. PerioGT-Lite (mem_112) DISPROVED this: 9 augmentation strategies tested across 4 iterations with perfect implementation consistency, none consistently beat baseline. The hypothesis was wrong — PA contrastive pre-training alone is insufficient even at PI1M scale.

The original PCR idea (mem_090, mem_104) hypothesized that monomer-trimer contrastive pairs would encode periodicity priors. PCR-v2 (mem_109) showed these pairs are EASY (cos_sim 0.94-0.97), providing no useful learning signal. The hypothesis assumed cross-size pairs would be structurally different enough to create meaningful contrastive tasks, but the shared substructure makes them trivially aligned. This is a fundamental mismatch between the physical intuition (different RU views should be different) and the empirical reality (shared encoder + shared substructure = naturally aligned).
alignment: MoCL's finding that domain-aware augmentation + global contrastive loss provides the best performance aligns with our finding that domain-specific pairs (monomer-trimer) are vastly superior to random augmentation (PCR-v2 Iteration 1: 54.03 vs 66.96). But MoCL's bioisostere substitution creates genuinely HARD positives (structurally different fragments with similar properties), while our monomer-trimer pairs are EASY (structurally similar fragments with identical properties). The lesson: domain-awareness is necessary but not sufficient — the augmentation must also create appropriate difficulty.

The contrastive difficulty trap connects to the Small-Graph Paradox (mem_097, mem_101): on small polymer graphs (30-60 nodes), simple GIN already captures local structure well. Contrastive pre-training can't add much because the architecture's expressiveness ceiling is limited by the small graph size, not by the initialization. Pre-training provides mild regularization (variance reduction) but not useful periodicity priors because simple GIN can't effectively USE them.

The statistical fluctuation warning (mem_114) aligns with the anti-self-deception principle: the 49.83 single-seed result was a -4% improvement that disappeared under multi-seed verification. This is now a MANDATORY requirement — always verify with ≥3 seeds before claiming improvement.
content.key_insight: The Contrastive Difficulty Trap is a three-zone problem: easy positives are redundant, hard positives cause negative transfer, and the sweet spot is too narrow and non-monotonic to be practical. This trap is ESPECIALLY severe for polymer graphs because: (1) the most natural positive pairs (monomer-trimer from same polymer) are trivially easy due to shared substructure, (2) creating genuinely hard positives requires augmentations that destroy chemical semantics (shifted-RU, monomer-dimer), and (3) the sweet spot augmentations (edge+feat masking at specific corruption levels) provide marginal, non-reproducible gains. The fundamental issue is that contrastive learning operates on EMBEDDING similarity, but what matters for polymer property prediction is PROPAGATION structure — how features flow across RUs. Contrastive invariance says 'different views should look similar at the embedding level,' but what we need is 'the model should understand how features propagate across the periodic chain.' These are different objectives, and the contrastive approach addresses the wrong one.

memory.abstract: Three Validated Failure Modes and the Architecture-Periodicity Encoding Mismatch: Architecture alone fails (GPS=54.41), generic SSL alone fails (JEPA collapsed, contrastive=50.77), PA contrastive pre-training alone fails (PerioGT-Lite=52.92 mean). The critical insight is that periodicity encoding is architecture-dependent: periodic edges benefit Chemprop (bond-level messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level messages). Simple GIN cannot USE pre-trained periodicity priors because its ceiling (~51 RMSE) is set by architecture expressiveness, not initialization quality. The 50→30 gap requires either matching periodicity encoding to architecture (Chemprop+periodic edges), using periodicity through fine-tuning strategy (PGFT), or encoding periodicity explicitly in features (path/distance encoding).
memory.keyword: three failure modes, architecture-periodicity mismatch, periodic edges, Chemprop, GIN, simple GIN ceiling, PGFT, path encoding, representation-usage gap

consensus: Three validated failure modes for the 50→30 gap (mem_113): (1) Architecture innovation alone fails — GPS-SPSE-Trimer=54.41 (Small-Graph Paradox: Transformer redundant on 30-60 node graphs). (2) Generic SSL alone fails — JEPA collapsed (mem_098), contrastive=50.77 (doesn't beat 50.19 baseline). (3) PA contrastive pre-training alone fails — PerioGT-Lite=52.92 mean across seeds (mem_112). None of these single-axis approaches close the gap.

The architecture-periodicity encoding mismatch (mem_108, mem_087): Antoniuk et al. shows that periodic edges benefit Chemprop (directed bond-level messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level messages). Our Day 1 experiment confirmed this: GIN+Cyclized=53.28 (worst) while Chemprop+polymer graph achieves best results. This means periodicity encoding via graph topology modification is NOT universal — it must match the architecture's message-passing mechanism. GIN's simple sum aggregation treats the periodic edge as a shortcut for memorization; Chemprop's directed bond messages properly propagate information through it.

The simple GIN ceiling (~51 RMSE) is now firmly established across multiple experiments: Day 1 GIN+Trimer=50.19 (sum_pool), PCR-v2 baseline=51.34 (mean_pool), PerioGT-Lite baseline=51.92-52.49 (mean_pool). Pre-training (PerioGT-Lite) does NOT break this ceiling — it provides variance reduction (std 0.29 vs 1.25) but not mean improvement. This confirms that the ceiling is architectural, not initialization-based: simple GIN on 30-60 node trimer graphs has a fixed expressiveness-regularization balance that cannot be shifted by better initialization.

PerioGT achieves 30.8 RMSE with THREE components: (a) GPS-style architecture (Transformer + MPNN), (b) PA-based contrastive pre-training on PI1M, (c) PGFT prompt-guided fine-tuning. We have tested (b) alone (PerioGT-Lite, FAILED) and (a) alone (GPS-SPSE, FAILED). The missing component is likely (c) PGFT — which uses pre-trained representations as conditioning signals (prompts) during fine-tuning, not just weight initialization. This fundamentally changes how pre-trained knowledge is utilized.
conflicts: The Day 2 Architecture-SSL Co-Design integration (mem_101) hypothesized that simple MPNN + PA contrastive pre-training was the validated path, citing PerioGT's success. Day 3 PerioGT-Lite (mem_112) disproved this: simple GIN + PA contrastive pre-training is NOT sufficient. The original co-design principle was PARTIALLY correct — the right combination exists (PerioGT achieves 30.8), but the specific implementation (simple GIN + PA contrastive) is wrong. The co-design must include PGFT or path encoding as the third component.

The Small-Graph Paradox (mem_097) says Transformer attention is redundant on polymer trimers, but PerioGT uses GPS-style Transformer+MPNN and achieves 30.8. This apparent contradiction resolves when noting that PerioGT's Transformer is PRE-TRAINED on PI1M — it doesn't learn from scratch on 7170 samples. Pre-trained Transformers have different behavior than randomly initialized ones: they provide structured global representations that complement local MPNN features, rather than redundant memorization. The Small-Graph Paradox applies to RANDOMLY INITIALIZED Transformers on small datasets, not to PRE-TRAINED Transformers that bring external knowledge.
alignment: The representation-usage gap aligns with MoCL's finding (mem_107) that domain-aware augmentation is essential but must create HARD positives. Our pre-training learns representations that reduce variance (mild regularization) but simple GIN can't USE them for Tg prediction because the architecture lacks the mechanism to integrate pre-trained periodicity knowledge into the supervised prediction. PGFT solves this by making the pre-trained representation a CONDITIONING SIGNAL rather than just an initialization — the model uses the pre-trained knowledge actively during fine-tuning.

The architecture-dependent periodicity encoding aligns with the Data-Centric Foundation integration (mem_087): data transformations are NOT universally beneficial — cyclization helps Chemprop but hurts GIN. The lesson extends: periodicity encoding (whether via graph topology, contrastive pre-training, or fine-tuning strategy) must be matched to the architecture's capabilities. Simple GIN needs periodicity encoded in FEATURES (path/distance encoding) or in FINE-TUNING STRATEGY (PGFT), not in graph topology or contrastive pre-training.

The three failure modes define a clear decision tree for Day 4 (mem_113): Option A (PGFT) addresses the representation-usage gap — pre-trained knowledge is used as conditioning, not initialization. Option B (path/distance encoding) addresses the feature gap — periodicity is encoded explicitly in node features. Option C (Chemprop+periodic edges) addresses the architecture-periodicity mismatch — matching periodicity encoding to architecture capabilities. Option D (BlochPoly, mem_106) addresses the fundamental gap — replacing implicit contrastive periodicity with explicit spectral decomposition.
content.key_insight: The 50→30 gap is NOT a single-axis problem (architecture, SSL, or pre-training alone). It is a REPRESENTATION-USAGE gap: simple GIN can be pre-trained to learn periodicity-aware representations, but it cannot USE those representations for Tg prediction because the architecture lacks mechanisms to integrate pre-trained knowledge into supervised predictions. PerioGT solves this through PGFT (prompt-guided fine-tuning), which makes pre-trained representations ACTIVE participants in fine-tuning rather than passive initialization. The path forward requires either: (a) PGFT to bridge the representation-usage gap, (b) path/distance encoding to provide explicit periodicity features that GIN can use, (c) Chemprop architecture that can properly use periodicity encoding via graph topology, or (d) BlochPoly-style explicit spectral decomposition that computes periodicity rather than learning it. All four options address the same root cause: the model must be able to USE periodicity information, not just LEARN it.

memory.abstract: MetaMethod Consolidation: Day 3 added five critical lessons — (1) Easy vs Hard Positive Pairs (monomer-trimer are EASY at cos_sim 0.94+), (2) Augmentation Difficulty Sweet Spot is too narrow (0.88-0.93) and non-monotonic, (3) Pre-training ≠ Better Representations (variance reduction only, no mean improvement), (4) Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding (periodic edges help Chemprop but hurt GIN), (5) Statistical Fluctuation Warning (single-seed 49.83 was a fluctuation). These lessons collectively redefine the research strategy: the simple GIN + contrastive paradigm is exhausted, and Day 4 must pivot to PGFT, path encoding, or fundamentally different approaches.
memory.keyword: MetaMethod consolidation, easy vs hard pairs, augmentation sweet spot, pre-training paradox, architecture-dependent periodicity, statistical fluctuation, paradigm exhaustion, pivot strategy

consensus: Five new MetaMethod lessons from Day 3 (mem_111, mem_114) consolidate into a coherent framework: (1) Easy vs Hard Positive Pairs: Contrastive learning needs HARD positives (structurally different but semantically equivalent). Monomer-trimer pairs are EASY (cos_sim 0.94-0.97) because shared encoder + shared substructure naturally aligns them. MoCL (mem_107) validates this with bioisostere substitution creating genuinely hard positives. (2) Augmentation Difficulty Sweet Spot: The cos_sim range 0.88-0.93 is the only zone where contrastive pre-training marginally helps, but it's too narrow (~0.05 range) and non-monotonic (40% corruption HURTS while 50% helps). This makes hyperparameter optimization impractical. (3) Pre-training ≠ Better Representations: PI1M-scale pre-training reduces variance (std 0.29 vs 1.25) but doesn't improve mean RMSE. Pre-training provides mild regularization, not useful periodicity priors for simple GIN. (4) Architecture-Dependent Periodicity Encoding: Periodic edges benefit Chemprop (bond-level messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level messages). Topological periodicity encoding is not universal. (5) Statistical Fluctuation Warning: The 49.83 single-seed result was a fluctuation that disappeared under multi-seed verification. ALWAYS verify with ≥3 seeds.

These five lessons collectively demonstrate that the simple GIN + contrastive pre-training paradigm is EXHAUSTED. Three days of experiments (GPS, JEPA, PCR-v2, PerioGT-Lite) have tested every variant of this paradigm: architecture innovation (Day 2), generic SSL (Day 2), in-training contrastive (Day 3), and PA contrastive pre-training (Day 3). All failed. The paradigm's ceiling (~51 RMSE) cannot be broken by any modification within this family.

The pivot strategy (mem_113, mem_114) identifies four options for Day 4: (A) PGFT prompt-guided fine-tuning — uses pre-trained representation as conditioning signal, not just initialization. This addresses the representation-usage gap identified in mem_116. (B) LiGhT-style path/distance encoding — explicit polymer topology encoding that doesn't require pre-training. This addresses the feature gap. (C) Chemprop + periodic edges — matching architecture to periodicity encoding. This addresses the architecture-periodicity mismatch. (D) BlochPoly — Bloch theorem spectral decomposition for periodic structures. This addresses the fundamental gap by replacing implicit contrastive periodicity with explicit spectral modeling.
conflicts: The original MetaMethod lesson 'Periodicity Priors are Essential' (mem_002, mem_100) stated that generic SSL provides regularization but not domain-specific knowledge, and PA augmentation is essential. Day 3 PerioGT-Lite (mem_112) REFINES this: PA augmentation IS essential for domain-specific knowledge, but simple GIN CANNOT USE that knowledge. The periodicity prior is learned (variance reduction confirms some structure is captured) but not utilized (mean RMSE unchanged). The lesson must be updated: 'Periodicity priors are essential, but the architecture must be capable of USING them — simple GIN is not.'

The 'High-ROI Experimentation' lesson (mem_002) said to shift strategy when incremental modifications fail. Day 3 confirms this wisdom: after 3 days of failed incremental modifications within the simple GIN + contrastive paradigm, we must pivot to fundamentally different approaches. The lesson is validated by the experimental evidence.
alignment: The anti-self-deception principles (mem_002, mem_111, mem_114) are consistently strengthened: (1) Zero fabrication — all negative results reported honestly. (2) Overfitting gap diagnostic — PCR models trained longer with lower train RMSE but worse test RMSE (mem_109). (3) Statistical fluctuation warning — single-seed 49.83 was a fluctuation, now MANDATORY to verify with ≥3 seeds. (4) Implementation consistency — BatchNorm+sum_pool catastrophic failure (mem_109 Iteration 2) reinforces this lesson.

The research habits (mem_002, mem_111) align: negative results are valuable (PCR-v2 and PerioGT-Lite failures prevent wasted effort on similar approaches), simple baselines are surprisingly strong (GIN+Trimer=50.19 remains unbeaten), and matching algorithms to physical reality is critical (periodicity encoding must match architecture).

The learning discipline (mem_002, mem_114) aligns: Periodicity Priors Essential lesson is refined (priors are essential but architecture must use them), Implementation Consistency is reinforced (perfect consistency in PerioGT-Lite but still no improvement — consistency is necessary but not sufficient), and a new lesson is added: Contrastive Pre-training on Simple GIN is Insufficient (9 strategies, 4 iterations, none consistently beat baseline).
content.key_insight: Day 3 marks a paradigm shift in the research strategy. The simple GIN + contrastive pre-training paradigm is exhausted after comprehensive testing across 3 days. The five MetaMethod lessons collectively redefine the problem: the 50→30 gap is not a pre-training problem or an architecture problem alone — it is a REPRESENTATION-USAGE problem. Simple GIN can learn periodicity-aware representations (variance reduction confirms this) but cannot USE them for Tg prediction (mean RMSE unchanged). The solution requires mechanisms that bridge this gap: PGFT (active use of pre-trained knowledge), path encoding (explicit periodicity features), Chemprop (architecture that can use periodicity via topology), or BlochPoly (explicit spectral computation). The research must pivot from 'how to learn periodicity' to 'how to USE periodicity' — this is the fundamental reframing that Day 3 demands.

memory.abstract: Prompt-Conditioned Fine-Tuning (PCFT): PGFT-inspired mechanism using frozen pre-trained monomer embeddings as active conditioning signals during trimer fine-tuning — directly addresses the representation-usage gap (H4) by making periodicity knowledge an explicit input rather than passive weight initialization
memory.keyword: PGFT, prompt conditioning, frozen encoder, representation-usage gap, dual-encoder, periodicity prompt

H: H4a (Representation-Usage Gap via Conditioning): The 50→30 gap is fundamentally a representation-USAGE gap, not a representation-LEARNING gap. PerioGT-Lite confirmed that PA contrastive pre-training produces periodicity-aware representations (variance reduction std 0.29 vs 1.25) but simple GIN cannot USE them when they serve only as weight initialization — fine-tuning updates destroy the periodicity structure as the encoder adapts to Tg prediction. PCFT solves this by making the pre-trained representation an ACTIVE, FIXED conditioning input (prompt) that the prediction head can directly access. The frozen pre-trained embedding h_pre encodes periodicity structure that never gets destroyed during fine-tuning because it's not updated. The fine-tuning encoder adapts to Tg prediction while the frozen prompt preserves periodicity context. This is analogous to prompt-tuning in NLP: the prompt conditions the model's behavior without changing the model weights.

H4b (Dual-Channel Information Flow): Tg prediction benefits from TWO distinct information channels: (1) Task-adapted features from the fine-tuning trimer encoder (h_task) — captures inter-RU structural details optimized for Tg prediction, and (2) Periodicity-aware features from the frozen monomer encoder (h_pre) — captures RU-level periodicity invariance that survives across the chain. The prediction head MLP(h_task ⊕ h_pre) can learn to weight these channels appropriately: rely more on h_task for structural details, rely more on h_pre for periodicity context. This dual-channel design is fundamentally different from single-encoder fine-tuning where periodicity and task adaptation compete for the same weight space.

H5-Compat (Architecture-Periodicity Compatibility): PCFT is compatible with ANY backbone architecture. The frozen prompt h_pre is computed from monomer (small graph, ~10-20 nodes) regardless of the fine-tuning architecture. This means we can use GIN for the fine-tuning encoder (scale-appropriate per Small-Graph Paradox) while still providing periodicity context through h_pre. The periodicity knowledge doesn't need to be encoded in the architecture (which caused GIN+Cyclized=53.28 failure) — it's provided as an external conditioning signal that bypasses the architecture's limitations.
X:
PCFT Architecture (dual-encoder with frozen prompt):

(a) Frozen Pre-trained Encoder (Encoder P): GIN (5 layers, hidden_dim=256, dropout=0.5, global_mean_pool) on MONOMER graph → h_pre ∈ R^256. This encoder is pre-trained on PI1M with PA contrastive learning (best augmentation: 50% edge+feat mask, cos_sim ~0.88 from PerioGT-Lite experiments) and then FROZEN — no gradient computation during fine-tuning. The monomer input (~10-20 nodes) is small and fast to process. h_pre is computed once per polymer and stored, avoiding repeated computation.

(b) Fine-tuning Encoder (Encoder T): GIN (5 layers, hidden_dim=256, dropout=0.5, global_mean_pool) on TRIMER graph → h_task ∈ R^256. This encoder is initialized from the SAME pre-trained weights as Encoder P but is ALLOWED TO UPDATE during fine-tuning. It adapts to Tg prediction on the trimer representation (validated from Day 1 as optimal input). The trimer input (~30-60 nodes) provides inter-RU structural context.

(c) Prediction Head: Tg = MLP_pred(h_task ⊕ h_pre) ∈ R. The MLP takes the 512-dim concatenated vector (256 from task-adapted features + 256 from periodicity prompt) and maps to Tg prediction. Architecture: Linear(512, 256) → ReLU → Linear(256, 128) → ReLU → Linear(128, 1). This head learns to combine both information channels optimally.

(d) Key Design Choice: Encoder P and Encoder T share the SAME GIN architecture (5 layers, 256 hidden, dropout 0.5, mean pool) but have SEPARATE weight copies. Encoder P weights are frozen (no gradient); Encoder T weights are fine-tuned. Total parameters: ~900K (2 × ~450K GIN) + ~130K (prediction head) = ~1M params. Very feasible on 11GB GPU.

Pre-training Phase (reuse PerioGT-Lite infrastructure):

Use the best PerioGT-Lite pre-training configuration: PA contrastive on PI1M (300K subset) with 50% edge+feature mask augmentation (cos_sim ~0.88, the only strategy that showed marginal single-seed improvement). InfoNCE loss, tau=0.07, projector: 2-layer MLP (256→128→64) with L2 norm. Mixed precision (FP16), gradient accumulation for effective batch=512. Pre-train for 50 epochs.

CRITICAL: After pre-training, DISCARD the projector (it was only for contrastive learning). The pre-trained GIN encoder produces 256-dim graph embeddings via global_mean_pool — these are h_pre.

After pre-training, compute h_pre for ALL 7170 polymers in the Tg dataset by forward-passing each monomer through the frozen encoder. Store these as a lookup table: polymer_id → h_pre ∈ R^256. This takes ~5 minutes (7170 monomers, ~10-20 nodes each, very fast).

Fine-tuning Phase (the novel PGFT mechanism):

For each training batch:
1. Sample 32 polymers
2. Load pre-computed h_pre for each polymer from the lookup table (NO forward pass through frozen encoder needed during training)
3. Forward-pass each polymer's trimer through Encoder T → h_task
4. Concatenate: h_combined = h_task ⊕ h_pre
5. Prediction: Tg_pred = MLP_pred(h_combined)
6. Loss: L = MSE(Tg_pred, Tg_true)

NO contrastive loss during fine-tuning — the periodicity knowledge is provided through h_pre, not through in-training regularization. This eliminates the augmentation difficulty sweet spot problem that plagued PerioGT-Lite.

Training protocol: seed=71, 72/8/20 split, patience=30, best by val RMSE. LR=1e-3 with cosine annealing. Batch_size=32. Standard early stopping.

Memory estimate: Encoder T (~450K params with gradients) + MLP_pred (~130K params with gradients) + h_pre lookup table (7170 × 256 × 4 bytes = ~7MB) = well within 11GB GPU.

Alternative Prompt Injection Mechanisms (test which USAGE mechanism works best):

(i) Prediction-level conditioning (default): Tg = MLP(h_task ⊕ h_pre) — simplest, h_pre conditions the prediction head directly
(ii) Feature-level conditioning: Add h_pre as a VIRTUAL NODE feature to the trimer graph before Encoder T processes it. The virtual node broadcasts h_pre to all atoms through message passing. This allows Encoder T to USE periodicity information during message passing, not just at prediction. Risk: Day 1 showed GIN+VN increases overfitting (53.78 RMSE), but here the VN carries FIXED pre-trained features (not learnable), which may reduce overfitting.
(iii) Attention-level conditioning (if using GPS backbone): Use h_pre as attention bias in Transformer layers. Not applicable for simple GIN but relevant if we later combine with GPS.
(iv) Residual conditioning: h_combined = h_task + α*h_pre (additive, not concatenative). Simpler prediction head (256-dim input instead of 512-dim). α is a learnable scalar that controls how much periodicity context to inject.

Key ablations:

(a) GIN+Trimer baseline (no pre-training, no prompt) — Day 1 ceiling = 50.19 (sum_pool) / ~52 (mean_pool)
(b) PCFT with random-init Encoder P (no pre-training, h_pre from randomly initialized GIN) — tests whether the PROMPT MECHANISM itself helps regardless of pre-training quality. If this works, the dual-encoder structure is beneficial even without periodicity priors.
(c) PCFT with PA pre-trained Encoder P (full model) — tests H4a+H4b: whether frozen periodicity prompt improves Tg prediction
(d) Standard fine-tuning (single encoder, pre-trained weights, end-to-end update) — this is PerioGT-Lite's approach, already FAILED (52.92 mean). Including as negative control.
(e) PCFT with frozen Encoder P + frozen Encoder T (both encoders frozen, only prediction head trainable) — tests whether the prediction head alone can learn to combine h_task and h_pre. Minimal fine-tuning, maximum periodicity preservation.
(f) PCFT with prediction-level vs feature-level conditioning (ablation ii vs i) — tests which prompt injection mechanism works best
(g) PCFT with residual vs concatenative conditioning (ablation iv vs i) — tests whether additive injection is sufficient
(h) Progressive pre-training scale: 100K vs 300K vs 500K PI1M for Encoder P — tests whether better pre-training improves h_pre quality and downstream PCFT performance

Multi-seed verification (MANDATORY per Day 3 lesson):

All results must be verified with ≥3 seeds before claiming improvement. The PerioGT-Lite single-seed 49.83 was a statistical fluctuation — PCFT must avoid this trap. Use seeds {42, 71, 123} for all ablations.

Diagnostic analyses:

1. h_pre quality assessment: Compute pairwise cosine similarities between h_pre vectors of different polymers. If all h_pre are nearly identical (cos_sim >0.95), the frozen encoder produces degenerate representations and PCFT won't help. If h_pre shows meaningful diversity (cos_sim 0.3-0.7 for different polymers, >0.8 for similar polymers), the periodicity prompt carries useful discriminative information.

2. h_task vs h_pre divergence during fine-tuning: Track cos_sim(h_task, h_pre) for the same polymer across training epochs. Should DECREASE from ~0.9 (same init weights) to ~0.3-0.5 as Encoder T adapts to Tg prediction. This divergence is DESIRABLE — it means the two channels provide complementary information.

3. Prediction head weight analysis: After training, examine MLP_pred weights to determine how much it relies on h_task vs h_pre. If the first layer weights heavily favor h_task dimensions (first 256), the periodicity prompt is not being used. If weights are balanced, both channels contribute.

4. Overfitting gap: PCFT should have overfitting gap <5 (compared to GIN+Trimer=8.90). The frozen h_pre provides fixed periodicity context that can't memorize training patterns, acting as regularization.
Y: If H4a correct: PCFT with PA pre-trained Encoder P (ablation c) should significantly outperform standard fine-tuning (ablation d, PerioGT-Lite=52.92 mean). Expected: PCFT → ~40-45 RMSE, standard fine-tuning → ~52.92. The ~10-point gap validates that MAKING PERIODICITY AN ACTIVE INPUT (not just initialization) bridges the representation-usage gap.

If H4b correct: PCFT should outperform GIN+Trimer baseline (ablation a) even with random-init Encoder P (ablation b). Expected: random-init PCFT → ~48-50 (small improvement from dual-encoder structure), PA pre-trained PCFT → ~40-45 (larger improvement from periodicity prompt). The dual-channel structure provides complementary information even without pre-training, but pre-training makes h_pre more informative.

If H5-Compat correct: PCFT with simple GIN backbone should achieve better results than any approach that encodes periodicity in graph topology (GIN+Cyclized=53.28). The prompt mechanism bypasses the architecture's limitations by providing periodicity as an external signal.

Expected best result: ~40-45 RMSE with PCFT + PA pre-trained Encoder P on 300K PI1M. This closes ~5-10 points of the 50→30 gap through the representation-usage mechanism. The remaining gap (40→30.8) likely requires (a) better pre-training quality (full 1M PI1M), (b) Chemprop backbone that can use periodicity through topology, or (c) combined PCFT + Chemprop approach.

If PCFT achieves ~35-38: MAJOR FINDING — the representation-usage gap accounts for most of the 50→30 gap. Frozen periodicity prompts are the key mechanism that PerioGT's PGFT provides. This validates H4 and suggests that combining PCFT with Chemprop could approach SOTA.

If PCFT achieves ~48-50 (marginal improvement): The prompt mechanism helps slightly but h_pre doesn't carry strong enough periodicity signal. PerioGT-Lite's variance reduction (std 0.29 vs 1.25) suggests h_pre has SOME structure but may not be discriminative enough for Tg prediction. Escalate to: (a) larger pre-training scale (1M PI1M), (b) Chemprop backbone for better architecture-periodicity match, or (c) BlochPoly spectral decomposition for explicit periodicity.

If PCFT with random-init Encoder P (ablation b) achieves ~50-52 (no improvement over baseline): The dual-encoder structure itself doesn't help. The improvement must come entirely from h_pre quality (pre-training). This means PCFT's value is entirely dependent on pre-training quality — if pre-training is weak, PCFT is useless.

If PCFT with frozen Encoder T (ablation e) achieves ~45-48: The prediction head alone can partially use h_pre and h_task, but Encoder T needs to adapt to Tg for optimal performance. Partial fine-tuning (freeze encoder, train head only) provides some improvement but full fine-tuning of Encoder T is needed for best results.

If feature-level conditioning (ablation f-ii) outperforms prediction-level conditioning (ablation f-i): Injecting h_pre during message passing is more effective than injecting at prediction. The GNN can integrate periodicity context into node-level representations, providing richer information to the prediction head. This would validate that periodicity should be used at the REPRESENTATION level, not just the PREDICTION level.

If prediction-level conditioning outperforms feature-level: The virtual node approach (feature-level) may increase overfitting despite h_pre being fixed, because the virtual node adds a pathway for memorization. Prediction-level conditioning is safer because h_pre only affects the final prediction, not intermediate representations.

Critical negative result to watch: If cos_sim(h_task, h_pre) stays >0.8 throughout fine-tuning, Encoder T is NOT adapting — it's essentially copying Encoder P's behavior. This means the dual-encoder design is redundant (both produce similar embeddings). Mitigation: increase LR for Encoder T, add dropout between h_task and h_pre in the prediction head, or use residual conditioning with learnable α.

memory.abstract: Chemprop-Polymer: Directed bond-level MPNN (Chemprop) on periodic polymer graph (trimer + periodic edge) — directly addresses the architecture-periodicity mismatch (H5) by using an architecture whose message-passing mechanism is naturally compatible with periodic edge topology, validated by Antoniuk et al.'s 20% RMSE improvement
memory.keyword: Chemprop, periodic edge, bond-level messages, architecture-periodicity match, polymer graph, directed MPNN

H: H5a (Architecture-Periodicity Compatibility): The 50→30 gap requires matching periodicity encoding to the architecture's message-passing mechanism. Antoniuk et al. (mem_108) demonstrated that periodic edges benefit Chemprop (directed bond-level messages) but hurt GIN (atom-level sum-aggregation). Our Day 1 experiment confirmed this: GIN+Cyclized=53.28 (worst result) while Chemprop+polymer graph achieves best results in the literature. The mechanism: Chemprop processes BONDS as directed messages (each bond has separate forward and backward message vectors), allowing the periodic edge to carry specific inter-RU coupling information. GIN processes ATOMS via sum-aggregation, treating the periodic edge as just another neighbor connection — creating a shortcut for memorization rather than a channel for periodicity propagation.

H5b (Bond-Level Messages Encode Inter-RU Coupling): In a periodic polymer, the inter-RU coupling is fundamentally a BOND-level phenomenon: the backbone bonds connecting one RU to the next (the star-bond connections in p-SMILES) determine how information propagates across the chain. Chemprop's directed bond messages naturally model this: each bond has a forward message (from atom i to atom j) and a reverse message (from atom j to atom i). The periodic edge between terminal atoms of the trimer gets its own directed messages, which can encode the specific chemistry of the inter-RU connection (e.g., C-C backbone bond vs. C-O backbone bond). This is far more informative than GIN's atom-level aggregation which treats the periodic edge as just another neighbor.

H5c (Chemprop + Periodic Edge is Sufficient Without Pre-training): Antoniuk et al. achieved ~20% RMSE improvement with Chemprop+polymer graph WITHOUT any pre-training — purely through architectural compatibility with periodicity encoding. This suggests that the representation-usage gap can be partially closed by simply using the right architecture-periodicity combination. The periodic edge provides EXPLICIT periodicity topology; Chemprop provides the architecture that can USE it. No contrastive pre-training, no prompt-guided fine-tuning, no spectral decomposition — just matching the encoding to the architecture. If this works on our Tg dataset, it provides the simplest validated path toward closing the 50→30 gap.
X:
Chemprop-Polymer Architecture:

(a) Polymer Graph Construction: For each polymer p-SMILES, construct a TRIMER graph (3 repeat units) and add a PERIODIC EDGE connecting the two terminal atoms. This is exactly the polymer graph from Antoniuk et al. (mem_108). The periodic edge ensures all atoms have their correct bonding environment and the representation is unique for different propagation sites.

Implementation: Use RDKit to parse p-SMILES, identify star atoms (*) and their connections, construct the trimer by concatenating 3 copies of the repeat unit, and add the periodic edge between the terminal atoms that would connect to the next RU in the infinite chain. This requires careful SMILES manipulation — the star atoms in the monomer become real bonds in the trimer, and the terminal atoms get the periodic edge.

(b) Chemprop MPNN Backbone: Use the standard Chemprop architecture (yang2019chemprop) with directed bond-level messages:
- Initialize learned atom features (dim=256) and bond features (dim=256) from RDKit descriptors
- 3 message-passing steps (T=3, as in Antoniuk et al.)
- Each step: for each bond (i→j), compute hidden bond message h_{ij} = MLP(h_i, h_j, h_{ji}, f_{ij}) where h_i, h_j are atom hidden states, h_{ji} is the reverse bond message, and f_{ij} are bond features
- After T steps, aggregate bond messages into atom hidden states, then global_mean_pool into graph encoding
- Feed through 2-layer FFN (256 neurons each) for Tg prediction

The PERIODIC EDGE is treated as a regular bond in Chemprop's message-passing: it gets its own forward and reverse message vectors, and its bond features encode that it's a periodic connection (special bond type flag). This allows Chemprop to learn how information propagates through the periodic boundary.

Implementation Details:

1. Chemprop library: Use the official chemprop Python package (https://github.com/chemprop/chemprop). It already implements directed bond-level MPNN with all necessary components.

2. Polymer graph preprocessing: Modify the p-SMILES → graph conversion to:
   - Parse p-SMILES, identify star atoms (*) and their bonding partners
   - Construct trimer by concatenating 3 RUs: replace [*] with actual bond to next RU's corresponding atom
   - Add periodic edge: connect the terminal atoms (the atoms that would bond to the 4th RU) with a special bond type (bond_type=7 or similar, to flag as periodic)
   - Store as standard molecular graph compatible with Chemprop's input format

3. Bond features for periodic edge: The periodic edge should have a SPECIAL bond feature flag (is_periodic=1) so Chemprop can distinguish it from regular covalent bonds. Other bond features (bond type, conjugation, ring membership) are set appropriately for the backbone connection type (single, double, etc.).

4. Atom features: Standard RDKit atom features (atomic number, degree, formal charge, hybridization, aromaticity, etc.) — same as Day 1 GIN features for fair comparison. No custom features needed; Chemprop learns its own feature embeddings.

Training Protocol:

- Dataset: 7170 Tg polymers, same seed=71, 72/8/20 split, patience=30, best by val RMSE
- Chemprop default hyperparameters: batch_size=50, LR=1e-4, epochs=100 (Chemprop uses different defaults than our GIN setup)
- BUT: adapt to our protocol for fair comparison: LR=1e-3, cosine annealing, patience=30, batch_size=32
- Multi-seed verification with ≥3 seeds (seeds {42, 71, 123}) — MANDATORY per Day 3 lesson

Memory estimate: Chemprop on trimer graphs (30-60 nodes, ~60-120 edges including periodic edge) with hidden_dim=256, 3 message-passing steps. Should be ~2-4MB per batch, well within 11GB GPU.

Key Ablations:

(a) Chemprop + monomer graph (no periodic edge, no trimer) — baseline for Chemprop architecture without periodicity encoding
(b) Chemprop + trimer graph (3 RUs, no periodic edge) — tests whether trimer representation helps with Chemprop (it should, per Day 1 finding that trimer > monomer)
(c) Chemprop + polymer graph (trimer + periodic edge) — FULL MODEL, tests H5a+H5b+H5c
(d) GIN + trimer (Day 1 baseline = 50.19) — architecture comparison: same data, different architecture
(e) GIN + polymer graph (Day 1 GIN+Cyclized = 53.28) — architecture comparison: same periodicity encoding, different architecture (negative control)
(f) Chemprop + polymer graph with periodic edge REMOVED during training (add periodic edge only during inference) — tests whether periodic edge information is used during message passing or only at inference
(g) Chemprop + polymer graph with random periodic edge (connect random terminal atoms instead of correct ones) — tests whether the SPECIFIC chemistry of the periodic edge matters or just having an extra connection helps
(h) Chemprop + trimer + PCFT prompt (combine Chemprop architecture with frozen periodicity prompt from Idea 1) — tests whether architectural compatibility + prompt conditioning are complementary

Diagnostic Analyses:

1. Bond message analysis for periodic edge: After training, extract the forward and reverse message vectors for the periodic edge across different polymers. If these messages show meaningful variation (different polymers have different periodic edge messages), Chemprop is USING the periodic edge to encode inter-RU coupling. If all periodic edge messages are similar, the periodic edge is not being utilized.

2. Ablation impact of periodic edge: Compare (c) vs (b) — the RMSE difference directly measures how much the periodic edge contributes. Antoniuk et al. found ~4% average improvement from periodic edge; we should see similar magnitude on Tg.

3. Architecture comparison: Compare (c) vs (d) — Chemprop+polymer vs GIN+trimer. The RMSE difference measures how much architecture-periodicity compatibility matters. Expected: Chemprop significantly outperforms GIN when both use their optimal data representation (Chemprop+polymer vs GIN+trimer).

4. Overfitting gap: Chemprop should have lower overfitting gap than GIN because (a) directed bond messages provide more structured information flow, and (b) the periodic edge provides explicit topology that constrains what the model can learn. Track train RMSE - test RMSE for all ablations.

Risk Assessment:

1. Chemprop may not improve over GIN+Trimer on our SPECIFIC Tg dataset. Antoniuk et al. tested on a different Tg dataset (7235 polymers from PolyInfo) and achieved 37.35 RMSE with polymer graph vs 39.83 with monomer graph. Their absolute numbers are much better than ours, suggesting their dataset may be easier or their training protocol different. Our GIN+Trimer=50.19 ceiling may persist even with Chemprop if the dataset difficulty dominates.

2. The periodic edge construction may introduce errors for some p-SMILES (e.g., polymers with complex branching, multiple star atoms). Need careful preprocessing validation.

3. Chemprop's default hyperparameters (LR=1e-4, batch=50) differ from our GIN protocol (LR=1e-3, batch=32). Need to decide whether to use Chemprop defaults (their validated settings) or our protocol (for fair comparison). Recommend: use Chemprop defaults first, then adapt if needed.

4. Memory: Chemprop processes directed bond messages, which doubles the message computation compared to GIN's atom-level messages. On trimer graphs with periodic edge (~120 directed bonds), this may be slightly more expensive but still feasible on 11GB GPU.
Y: If H5a correct: Chemprop+polymer graph (ablation c) should significantly outperform GIN+polymer graph (ablation e, 53.28). Expected: Chemprop+polymer → ~42-48, GIN+polymer → ~53.28. The ~10-point gap validates that architecture-periodicity compatibility is critical — the same periodicity encoding helps with Chemprop but hurts with GIN.

If H5b correct: Bond message analysis should show that periodic edge messages carry meaningful inter-RU coupling information. Different backbone types (C-C, C-O, C-N) should produce different periodic edge messages. If periodic edge messages are uniform across polymers, the architecture isn't leveraging the periodic edge's chemistry.

If H5c correct: Chemprop+polymer WITHOUT pre-training should achieve meaningful improvement over GIN+trimer baseline (50.19). Expected: ~42-48 RMSE. This would close ~5-10 points of the 50→30 gap purely through architecture-periodicity matching, without any pre-training infrastructure. This is the SIMPLEST validated path.

Expected best result: ~42-48 RMSE with Chemprop+polymer graph (no pre-training). This closes 5-10 points of the gap through architectural compatibility. The remaining gap (42→30.8) likely requires combining Chemprop with (a) PA contrastive pre-training, (b) PCFT prompt conditioning, or (c) both.

If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~38-42: Strong improvement, approaching the range where combining with PCFT or pre-training could reach SOTA. This validates H5 and makes Chemprop the preferred backbone for all future experiments.

If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~48-50 (only marginal improvement over GIN+trimer=50.19): Architecture-periodicity compatibility helps but is not sufficient. The Tg dataset difficulty dominates, and the gap requires pre-training + prompt conditioning on top of architectural compatibility.

If Chemprop+polymer achieves >50 (no improvement): Chemprop doesn't help on our Tg dataset. Possible reasons: (a) our Tg dataset is harder than Antoniuk et al.'s, (b) Chemprop's directed bond messages don't provide enough additional expressiveness for Tg prediction, (c) the periodic edge construction has errors. This would be a surprising negative result given the literature evidence.

If Chemprop+monomer (ablation a) achieves ~48-52: Chemprop alone (without periodicity encoding) is comparable to GIN+trimer. The architecture itself doesn't provide a major advantage — the improvement comes from the COMBINATION of Chemprop architecture + periodic edge topology.

If Chemprop+trimer (ablation b, no periodic edge) achieves ~46-48: Trimer representation helps Chemprop (consistent with Day 1 finding), but the periodic edge provides additional ~2-4 RMSE improvement (consistent with Antoniuk et al.'s ~4% finding).

If random periodic edge (ablation g) performs similarly to correct periodic edge: The SPECIFIC chemistry of the periodic connection doesn't matter — just having an extra connection helps Chemprop by increasing connectivity. This would weaken H5b and suggest the improvement is from graph topology (more edges = more information flow) rather than from periodicity encoding.

If Chemprop+polymer+PCFT (ablation h) achieves ~35-38: Architecture-periodicity compatibility + prompt conditioning are COMPLEMENTARY. Chemprop provides the right architecture for periodicity; PCFT provides the right mechanism for using pre-trained periodicity knowledge. This combination could approach SOTA.

Progressive strategy: If Chemprop+polymer achieves ~42-48, the next step is to add PCFT (Idea 1) on top — using Chemprop as the fine-tuning backbone instead of GIN, with frozen pre-trained monomer embeddings as periodicity prompts. This combines architectural compatibility (H5) with representation-usage mechanism (H4) for maximum effect.

memory.abstract: BlochSpec: Computing Bloch band structure of chemistry-weighted periodic Laplacian as deterministic input features — shifts periodicity from representation space (learned, can't be used by GIN) to input space (computed, naturally usable by any architecture), bypassing the representation-usage gap entirely without contrastive pre-training
memory.keyword: Bloch band structure, chemistry-weighted Laplacian, deterministic spectral features, input-space periodicity, representation-usage gap bypass

H: H1 (Input-Space Periodicity Bypasses Representation-Usage Gap): The 50→30 gap is a representation-USAGE gap: simple GIN can learn periodicity-aware representations (PerioGT-Lite variance reduction confirms) but cannot USE them for Tg prediction because learned periodicity resides in the representation space where fine-tuning destroys it. BlochSpec bypasses this entirely by shifting periodicity to the INPUT space — computing the Bloch band structure of the polymer's chemistry-weighted periodic Laplacian as deterministic features that are concatenated with the GNN embedding. Any architecture naturally processes input features through its standard computational path (message passing → pooling → prediction); no special mechanism (PGFT, periodic edges, contrastive pre-training) is needed. The GNN doesn't need to LEARN periodicity — it's GIVEN as physics-derived input. This is the fundamental paradigm shift: from 'how to teach the model periodicity' to 'how to give the model computed periodicity.'

H2 (Bloch Band Structure Encodes Tg-Relevant Physics): The Bloch band structure E_n(k) of a 1D periodic chain directly encodes the physical determinants of Tg: (a) Spectral gap (gap between lowest eigenvalues at k=0) → chain connectivity/rigidity. Polymers with large spectral gaps have well-connected, rigid backbones → high Tg. (b) Low-frequency mode density (number of eigenvalues near zero across k) → chain flexibility. Polymers with many near-zero modes have flexible chains → low Tg. (c) Band width (spread of E_n(k) across k for each band n) → inter-RU coupling strength. Wide bands mean features propagate strongly across RUs → chain-level effects dominate. (d) Spectral radius (maximum eigenvalue) → overall coupling strength including intermolecular interactions. These spectral summaries are COMPACT (~8-12 features) and PHYSICS-INFORMED — they directly encode the periodicity structure that determines macroscopic properties, unlike contrastive invariance which only says 'different views should look similar.'

H3 (Chemistry-Weighted Laplacian Captures Both Topology and Chemistry): The standard graph Laplacian L = D - A only encodes connectivity, losing all chemical information (bond types, atom electronegativity, aromaticity). The chemistry-weighted Laplacian L_w = D_w - W incorporates: (a) Edge weights from bond chemistry: single=1.0, double=2.0, aromatic=1.5, triple=3.0, plus electronegativity difference between bonded atoms (captures bond polarity). (b) The periodic edge weight set to the backbone bond type at the RU boundary — this is the crucial inter-RU coupling that determines propagation. (c) Node weights from atom chemistry: electronegativity, degree, hybridization encoded as diagonal modifications. The resulting Bloch band structure E_n(k) of L_w encodes BOTH periodic topology AND chemistry — the spectral features are not just 'how connected is the chain' but 'how do chemical features propagate across the periodic chain.' This is why chemistry-weighting is essential: a C-C backbone and a C-O backbone have different coupling weights, producing different band structures that reflect their different Tg-relevant physics.
X:
BlochSpec Architecture (computed spectral features + standard GIN, NO pre-training):

(a) Spectral Feature Computation (deterministic, no learning):

Step 1: Chemistry-Weighted Laplacian Construction
For each polymer p-SMILES:
- Parse with RDKit, identify atoms, bonds, and star atoms (*)
- Construct monomer unit cell graph: N atoms, edges with chemistry-derived weights
- Edge weight w_ij = bond_type_weight × (1 + |Δ electronegativity|) where bond_type_weight = {1.0: single, 2.0: double, 1.5: aromatic, 3.0: triple} and Δ electronegativity captures bond polarity
- Identify boundary atoms (connected to star atoms): typically 2-4 atoms per monomer
- Construct coupling matrix L_coupling: N×N matrix, nonzero only for boundary atoms connecting to adjacent RUs. Coupling weight = backbone bond type weight (the chemistry of the inter-RU connection)
- Construct unit cell Laplacian L_UC: N×N chemistry-weighted Laplacian of the monomer

Step 2: Bloch Band Structure Computation
For k ∈ {0, π/12, π/6, ..., 2π-π/12} (24 sample k-points):
- Bloch Hamiltonian: H(k) = L_UC + e^{ik}·L_coupling + e^{-ik}·L_coupling^T
- Compute eigenvalues: λ_1(k), λ_2(k), ..., λ_N(k) via numpy.linalg.eigvalsh (symmetric matrix, real eigenvalues)
- This gives N×24 = 24N eigenvalue points forming the Bloch band structure
- For N≈10-20 atoms: 240-480 eigenvalue points per polymer

Step 3: Compact Spectral Summary Extraction
From the 24N eigenvalue points, compute ~10-12 summary features:
1. spectral_gap = λ_2(0) - λ_1(0) (chain connectivity)
2. spectral_radius = max(λ_n(k)) across all n,k (overall coupling)
3. spectral_centroid = mean(λ_n(k)) (average coupling)
4. spectral_variance = std(λ_n(k)) (coupling diversity)
5. low_freq_density = count(λ_n(k) < 0.5) / (N×24) (chain flexibility)
6. band_width_max = max over n of (max_k λ_n(k) - min_k λ_n(k)) (strongest inter-RU coupling)
7. band_width_mean = mean over n of (max_k λ_n(k) - min_k λ_n(k)) (average inter-RU coupling)
8. band_flatness = mean over n of (1 - band_width_n / centroid_n) (mode localization)
9. spectral_gap_kpi = min over k of (λ_{n+1}(k) - λ_n(k)) for the largest gap (band gap analog)
10. density_at_Fermi = count(|λ_n(k) - λ_median| < 0.3) / (N×24) (states near median energy)
11. participation_ratio = mean over n of (Σ_k |ψ_n(k)|^4)^{-1} / (24) (mode delocalization)

These 10-12 features are COMPACT, PHYSICS-INFORMED, and DETERMINISTIC.

Step 4: Node-Level Bloch Participation Vectors (optional, more radical)
For each atom i in the trimer graph:
- Compute participation in top-3 Bloch modes: p_i = [|ψ_1(k*,i)|², |ψ_2(k*,i)|², |ψ_3(k*,i)|²] where k* is the k-point with largest spectral gap
- This 3-dimensional vector tells each atom 'you participate strongly in propagation mode 1' or 'you're confined to the unit cell'
- Concatenate p_i with standard atom features (atomic number, degree, etc.) as INPUT to the GNN
- This gives the GNN node-level periodicity information during message passing

Total preprocessing time: ~2 seconds for all 7170 polymers (numpy operations on 10-20×10-20 matrices). No GPU needed.

(b) GNN Architecture (standard, NO changes to message passing):

GIN (3 layers, hidden_dim=256, global_add_pool) on TRIMER graph → h_gnn ∈ R^256
- Same architecture as Day 1 baseline (3-layer GIN + sum_pool + trimer = 50.19)
- NO periodic edges in the trimer (avoid GIN+Cyclized=53.28 failure)
- NO pre-training (avoid PerioGT-Lite/PCR-v2 failures)
- NO contrastive loss (avoid augmentation difficulty trap)
- Standard atom features + optional Bloch participation vectors as node-level features

(c) Prediction Head:
Tg = MLP_pred(h_gnn ⊕ spectral_summary) ∈ R
- h_gnn: 256-dim GNN embedding (captures local structure via message passing)
- spectral_summary: 10-12 dim computed Bloch features (captures periodicity via physics)
- MLP: Linear(268, 128) → ReLU → Linear(128, 1)
- Total input dimension: 256 + 12 = 268 (minimal increase over baseline 256)

(d) Physics-Informed Regularization (optional, encodes known Tg-spectral relationship):
L_physics = MSE(Tg_pred, Tg_true) + β · ReLU(-∂Tg_pred/∂spectral_gap) 
This encourages monotonicity: larger spectral gap → higher Tg (rigid chain → high Tg).
β ramped from 0 to 0.01 over training. This is a SOFT constraint, not a hard rule — some polymers may violate monotonicity due to side-chain effects.

(e) Training Protocol:
- seed=71, 72/8/20 split, patience=30, best by val RMSE
- LR=1e-3, cosine annealing, batch_size=32
- Same protocol as Day 1 for fair comparison
- Multi-seed verification (≥3 seeds: {42, 71, 123}) MANDATORY
- Estimated training time: ~30 minutes (same as Day 1 GIN+Trimer)

RADICAL ABLATION: Pure Spectral MLP (no GNN at all):

Tg = MLP_pure(spectral_summary) ∈ R
- Input: only the 10-12 computed Bloch spectral features
- MLP: Linear(12, 64) → ReLU → Linear(64, 32) → ReLU → Linear(32, 1)
- This tests whether the Bloch spectral features alone are sufficient for Tg prediction
- If this achieves ~45-50 RMSE: spectral features capture most Tg-relevant information, GNN adds marginal value
- If this achieves >60 RMSE: spectral features alone are insufficient, GNN local structure is essential
- This ablation is the most conceptually radical: it replaces the entire GNN paradigm with physics-computed features

Implementation: Pre-compute all spectral features once (~2 seconds), store as numpy arrays. During training, load spectral features + graph data per batch. No architectural complexity.

Key Ablations (all with multi-seed verification):

(a) GIN+Trimer baseline (Day 1, no spectral features) = 50.19 — reference ceiling
(b) GIN+Trimer + Bloch spectral summaries (graph-level injection) — FULL MODEL, tests H1+H2+H3
(c) GIN+Trimer + node-level Bloch participation vectors (node-level injection) — tests whether node-level periodicity is more effective than graph-level
(d) GIN+Trimer + BOTH graph-level summaries + node-level participation — maximum spectral injection
(e) Pure Spectral MLP (no GNN) — radical ablation, tests whether GNN is needed at all
(f) GIN+Trimer + RANDOM spectral features (same dimension, random values) — tests whether the SPECIFIC physics-derived features matter vs. just having more features
(g) GIN+Trimer + standard Laplacian eigenvalues (unweighted, no chemistry) — tests H3: whether chemistry-weighting is essential
(h) GIN+Trimer + LapPE (standard Laplacian positional encoding from trimer, no periodicity) — tests whether Bloch band structure is better than standard spectral encoding
(i) GIN+Trimer + SPSE (path-based structural encoding from trimer) — Day 2 already tested this in GPS context (54.41), but worth testing with simple GIN
(j) GIN+Cyclized + Bloch spectral summaries — tests whether spectral features help even with the problematic cyclized topology
(k) GIN+Trimer + Bloch spectral + physics-informed monotonicity loss — tests whether soft physical constraints help
(l) Chemprop+Polymer graph + Bloch spectral summaries — combines architecture-periodicity match (mem_119) with computed spectral features
Y: If H1 correct: BlochSpec (ablation b) should significantly outperform GIN+Trimer baseline (ablation a, 50.19). Expected: ~42-48 RMSE. The computed spectral features provide periodicity information in the INPUT space that the GNN can naturally use through message passing, bypassing the representation-usage gap. This improvement should be LARGER than what contrastive pre-training provides (PerioGT-Lite: 0 improvement in mean RMSE) because computed features are deterministic and architecture-independent, while learned representations are architecture-specific and destroyed during fine-tuning.

If H2 correct: (a) The spectral gap should show positive correlation with Tg across the dataset (rigid chains → high Tg). Pearson r > 0.3 would validate the physics connection. (b) Low-frequency density should show negative correlation with Tg (flexible chains → low Tg). (c) Band width should correlate with Tg for polymers where inter-RU coupling matters (e.g., polar backbone polymers). These correlations can be checked BEFORE training — if they exist, the spectral features carry Tg-relevant signal. If correlations are weak (r < 0.1), the spectral features may not be informative enough and H2 is partially wrong.

If H3 correct: Chemistry-weighted spectral features (ablation b) should outperform unweighted spectral features (ablation g). Expected: chemistry-weighted → ~42-48, unweighted → ~48-50. The chemistry weighting makes the band structure encode bond polarity and backbone type, which are Tg-relevant. Unweighted Laplacian only encodes connectivity, missing the chemical determinants of inter-RU coupling.

If the FULL MODEL (ablation b) achieves ~42-45: Meaningful improvement (~5-8 points over baseline), validating H1. The representation-usage gap is partially bridged by shifting periodicity to input space. Remaining gap (42→30.8) likely requires combining with Chemprop architecture or PGFT-style conditioning.

If the FULL MODEL achieves ~38-42: Strong improvement (~8-12 points), suggesting computed spectral features capture significant Tg-relevant periodicity information. This would be a major finding: deterministic physics-computed features outperform learned contrastive representations for periodicity encoding.

If the FULL MODEL achieves ~35-38: Near-SOTA improvement, suggesting the Bloch band structure captures most Tg-relevant physics. The remaining gap may be addressable with node-level participation vectors or physics-informed loss. This would validate that the representation-usage gap is primarily about WHERE periodicity is encoded (input vs. representation), not about HOW it's learned.

If the FULL MODEL achieves >50 (no improvement): Computed spectral features don't help simple GIN. Possible reasons: (a) the spectral summaries are too compact and lose critical information, (b) the chemistry-weighted Laplacian construction has errors, (c) GIN message passing can't effectively integrate graph-level spectral features with node-level representations. Mitigation: try node-level injection (ablation c) instead of graph-level.

If node-level Bloch participation (ablation c) outperforms graph-level summaries (ablation b): Node-level periodicity information is more effective because it's processed during message passing, allowing atoms to communicate their propagation mode participation to neighbors. Graph-level features only affect the prediction head, missing the opportunity for periodicity-aware message passing. This would suggest that periodicity should be injected at the NODE level, not the GRAPH level — a key design insight.

If BOTH node-level + graph-level (ablation d) significantly outperforms either alone: The two injection levels are complementary — node-level features enable periodicity-aware message passing while graph-level features provide chain-level spectral context. This would be the optimal design.

If Pure Spectral MLP (ablation e) achieves ~45-50: The Bloch spectral features alone capture substantial Tg-relevant information. The GNN adds ~5-8 RMSE points of local structural detail. This validates H2 strongly — the band structure IS the physics that determines Tg.

If Pure Spectral MLP achieves ~55-60: Spectral features alone are insufficient. The GNN's local message passing captures essential non-spectral structural information (specific atom arrangements, ring structures, side-chain topology). The spectral features provide periodicity context that complements but cannot replace local structure.

If Pure Spectral MLP achieves >65: Spectral features are nearly useless alone. The compact summaries lose too much information. Need richer spectral representation (more features, eigenvector components) or the GNN is essential for any reasonable prediction.

If RANDOM spectral features (ablation f) achieve similar performance to real spectral features (ablation b): The improvement comes from having MORE input features (dimensionality increase), not from the SPECIFIC physics-derived content. This would invalidate H1 and H2 — the spectral features aren't carrying periodicity information, they're just adding parameters. Mitigation: reduce MLP hidden dims to control for parameter count.

If standard LapPE (ablation h) performs similarly to Bloch spectral (ablation b): The improvement comes from general spectral encoding, not from periodicity-specific Bloch decomposition. Standard Laplacian eigenvalues of the trimer (without periodicity) provide similar information. This weakens H2 — the periodicity-specific computation isn't adding value over general spectral features.

If Bloch spectral significantly outperforms LapPE: The Bloch band structure specifically encodes periodicity (inter-RU coupling through the coupling matrix) that standard LapPE (computed on the trimer without periodic edge) misses. This validates H2 — periodicity-specific spectral computation is essential.

Diagnostic: Pre-training correlation analysis — BEFORE any model training, compute Pearson correlations between each spectral summary feature and Tg across the 7170 dataset. Features with |r| > 0.2 carry Tg-relevant signal. Features with |r| < 0.05 are likely uninformative and can be dropped. This is a UNIQUE advantage of computed features: we can assess their relevance BEFORE training, unlike learned representations whose relevance is only revealed through downstream performance.

Overfitting gap diagnostic: BlochSpec should have overfitting gap comparable to or better than GIN+Trimer (8.90). The 10-12 deterministic spectral features cannot memorize training patterns (they're fixed computations), providing implicit regularization. If overfitting gap increases, the spectral features are enabling memorization through the prediction head — need to reduce MLP complexity or add dropout.

Progressive feature analysis: Start with the single most correlated spectral feature (e.g., spectral_gap), train GIN+Trimer+1_feature, measure RMSE. Then add features one by one in order of correlation strength. This reveals the MINIMUM set of spectral features needed for improvement and whether there's a diminishing returns threshold. Expected: first 3-4 features provide most of the improvement, additional features add marginal value.
